clue.text: Evil originally seen in Jack the Ripper's work?

indicators.note: seen in says the opening letter sits inside the sailor's word

parts.note: a jack, or jack tar, is an old name for a sailor, a tar

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the word Evil

explanation.surface: A wondering aside about the wickedness behind the Victorian murderer's handiwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack the Ripper' reads as one name, but Jack is the sailor and 'Ripper's work' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A ripper rips things, and a rip in cloth is also called this, so it is the ripper's handiwork.

clue.text: View of the 18 protagonist getting caught, not run out

indicators.note: not says the run-out letters are dropped and the caught letters take their place

parts.note: 18 across is TEMPESTS; the protagonist of Shakespeare's The Tempest is the magician Prospero
RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out
CT is a cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A cricket scorecard note about Shakespeare's magician: caught, not run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' joins the caught letters onto the name; 'not' removes RO.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is a wide view or vista, as from a hilltop.

clue.text: Fool commonly eats guts of fat bird as delicacy

indicators.note: eats means the slang word swallows the middle letters

parts.note: in common British slang a fool is called a tit

indicators.note: guts of takes the inner three letters of the phrase fat bird

explanation.surface: An idiot gobbles the innards of a plump bird, regarding them as a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guts of' picks TBI, the middle three letters of 'fat bird' run together.
explanation.definitionFit: A titbit is a small tasty morsel of food, a dainty treat.

clue.text: Flower seller's first flower show in Covent Garden?

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Fal is a river in Cornwall

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the word seller's

parts.note: again a river: the Taff flows through Cardiff in Wales

explanation.surface: A florist's opening floral display at London's old flower market in Covent Garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden was London's flower market and is home to the Royal Opera House, where Verdi's opera Falstaff is staged.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's opera of that name is staged at the Royal Opera House in Covent Garden.

clue.text: In drunken state outside 10, with glass full to the brim?

definitions.text: with glass full to the brim?

indicators.note: outside says the shuffled letters go round the other piece
drunken signals the letters of state reeling into a new order

parts.note: 10 across is BOARSHEAD, read as boar's head, the first letter of boar

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy beside the pub of 10 across, with a brimming glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunken' rearranges STATE to ATEST, which goes round B; 'In' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic: an optimist sees the glass full, so things viewed in the most favourable light.

clue.text: Acting on day lost for words

parts.note: A is a common abbreviation for acting, as in an acting manager
WED is the short form of Wednesday

explanation.surface: Performing on the night, an actor dries up completely.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone filled with wonder or reverence is often left speechless.

clue.text: Gaunt son in hospital, briefly very sick

indicators.note: sick means the letters of in and very are disordered

parts.note: in and very as written, with H, the short form for hospital, between them

explanation.surface: A gaunt young man in hospital, feeling very ill for a short time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaunt' looks like an adjective, but it is John of Gaunt; 'sick' rearranges IN, H and VERY together.
explanation.definitionFit: John of Gaunt's son Bolingbroke took the throne as this king, title of Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Time on leave: endless misery, having bit one's other half?

indicators.note: on means the time letter comes after the leave word

parts.note: to part is to leave or go away

indicators.note: endless means the misery word loses its last letter

parts.note: woe is misery

explanation.surface: Time off work, with endless misery, having bitten one's partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Henry IV has Part One and Part Two; with the first bit (Part One) done, the other half remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-part play's second instalment is the other half to the first.

clue.text: Supports breaks regularly offered by 10

indicators.note: offered by puts the 10 across letter before the alternating letters

parts.note: 10 across is BOARSHEAD, read as boar's head, the first letter of boar

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of breaks, the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: A pub offers support breaks at regular intervals.
explanation.definitionFit: Brassieres are undergarments that support the breasts.

clue.text: Pub to which Spooner's working girl retired

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words have their starts exchanged

parts.note: a working girl is a euphemism for a prostitute, a whore
to retire is to go to bed

explanation.surface: The tavern where a prostitute went to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Whore's bed, with its starting sounds swapped, gives boar's head. The Boar's Head in Eastcheap is Falstaff's haunt in Henry IV.
explanation.definitionFit: The Boar's Head is the Eastcheap tavern in Henry IV where Falstaff drinks.

clue.text: Film horrible short adult that's incontinent

indicators.note: that's, with the in- of incontinent, says the pieces are placed inside the continent

parts.note: split as in continent: Asia is a continent, and the pieces go in it

indicators.note: short means the horrible word loses its last letter

parts.note: nasty means horrible
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: Panning a film as dreadful, brief and adult, with a toilet joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incontinent' reads as one word but splits as 'in continent', so NASTA goes inside ASIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Anastasia is a film title, both the 1956 Ingrid Bergman drama and the 1997 animation.

clue.text: Page? He's in a group

indicators.note: in places the pronoun inside the group word

parts.note: a set is a group
the clue's He's, he is, gives HE

explanation.surface: Asking about a pageboy, who belongs to a band.
explanation.definitionFit: A page is one leaf of paper, so it can be called a sheet.

clue.text: Gin topless dancer's drunk without coke

indicators.note: drunk signals the remaining letters being jumbled
without means the coke letter is removed
topless means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: the clue's dancer's, letters DANCERS
C is slang shorthand for cocaine, coke

explanation.surface: A seedy bar scene: a topless dancer drinking gin with no mixer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' drops D, leaving ANCERS; 'without' removes C, leaving ANERS, which 'drunk' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin is a trap for catching animals, as a snare is.

clue.text: A comic drinks one can in store

indicators.note: drinks means the comic swallows the other letters

parts.note: a wag is a joker, a comic
I is the Roman numeral one
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A comedian downing a single canned drink kept in the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in store is lying ahead, still waiting to happen.

clue.text: Small number in 10 upset group of players

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the whole is read upwards, backwards
in puts the number abbreviation inside the ten

parts.note: here 10 is taken as the plain number ten, not a reference to 10 across
NO is the short form for number

explanation.surface: A small number in the pub of 10 across upsets a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 looks like a cross-reference to the pub but here is just the number; 'upset' reads the whole backwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is an ensemble of nine musicians.

clue.text: Ugly lump in conflict with model

parts.note: war is armed conflict
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T

explanation.surface: A disfiguring lump fighting with a fashion model.
explanation.definitionFit: A wart is an unsightly small growth on the skin.

clue.text: Witty remark, providing theme

parts.note: a mot, as in bon mot, is a witty remark
if means providing, as a condition

explanation.surface: A clever quip, provided it suits the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring idea or subject in a work.

clue.text: Bit on the side? Lock phone card up first

indicators.note: first puts the card word before the lock word
up in a down clue means the card word is read upwards

parts.note: a SIM is the card in a mobile phone
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Instructions about an affair: lock your phone and put the card away.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's bit on the side is his secret lover, his illicit partner.

clue.text: Tooth fairy's first name, inscribed in silver

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of fairy's
inscribed in means the name abbreviation is written inside the silver symbol

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: The tooth fairy's first name engraved on a silver keepsake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tooth fairy' reads as one thing; Tooth is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A fang is a long pointed tooth, as of a snake or dog.

clue.text: Guardian secretary in KFC ordered two items less than perfect order, stomach-wise?

definitions.text: two items less than perfect order, stomach-wise?

indicators.note: in places the paper's word and secretary inside the jumbled letters
ordered says the letters of KFC are rearranged

parts.note: the Guardian setter writes of the paper as ours, so Guardian gives OUR
PA is a personal assistant, a secretary

explanation.surface: The Guardian's secretary orders food at KFC, getting two items short.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perfect order, stomach-wise' is a six-pack of abdominal muscles; two fewer is a four-pack.
explanation.definitionFit: A six-pack is the ideal belly; take away two cans and you have a smaller bundle of drinks.

clue.text: Came across retired people causing trouble, coming to violent blows

indicators.note: retired means the word goes back, read backwards

parts.note: met means came across, encountered
pests are troublemakers

explanation.surface: Bumping into old troublemakers in retirement and ending up in a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming to violent blows' reads as a fight, but 'violent blows' are storms; 'coming to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempests are violent storms, blows of wind.

clue.text: Rod, after a great deal to drink, falls over

indicators.note: falls over means the combined letters are upended, read backwards in this down clue
after puts the drink word after the great deal word

parts.note: a lot is a great deal
to sip is to drink

explanation.surface: A man named Rod, after a huge amount to drink, topples over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like a man's name but is US slang for a gun; Pistol is also Falstaff's crony in Henry IV.
explanation.definitionFit: Rod is old American slang for a handgun.

clue.text: Spy eating a French sandwich

indicators.note: eating means the sandwich takes in the French article

parts.note: a BLT is a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich
un is French for a

explanation.surface: A secret agent having a French sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Blunt was a Soviet spy in the Cambridge Five ring.

clue.text: Quarrel where vehicle gets rammed?

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle
a tup is a ram, a male sheep, so a vehicle getting rammed is one that gets a tup

explanation.surface: An argument over a road accident in which a bus was hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets rammed' suggests a collision, but the vehicle literally gets a ram; 'where' and 'gets' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust-up is a noisy row or quarrel.

clue.text: As a turn is played in Haydn and Schubert?

indicators.note: played suggests the letters being performed in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: How a musical turn, an ornament, is performed in the works of two composers.
explanation.definitionFit: Haydn and Schubert were both born in Austria, so they are examples of its nationals.

clue.text: Book of plays

definitions.meaning: the ... of the Apostles is a book of the New Testament
plays as a verb, performs on stage

explanation.definitionFit: Acts is the Bible book after the Gospels, and one acts a part on stage.

clue.text: Power bills for flats

parts.note: bills are posters or advertisements, ads

explanation.surface: Electricity charges for the apartments.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad is slang for a flat or home.

clue.text: Toy Manx sheep?

indicators.note: a Manx cat has no tail, so Manx means the sheep's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Dolly was the famous cloned sheep

explanation.surface: A toy sheep from the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: A doll is a child's plaything shaped like a person.

clue.text: 8's not begun, surprisingly, with glass completely empty?

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the remaining letters being rearranged
not begun means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: 8 across with the 's gives the letters of that answer plus S

explanation.surface: The sequel unstarted, unexpectedly, with an empty glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not begun' drops P from PARTTWOS, leaving ARTTWOS; 'surprisingly' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic: the pessimist sees the glass empty, so things in the least favourable light.

clue.text: Queen getting weak, beheaded at once

parts.note: QU is a short form for queen, used in crosswords and old abbreviations

indicators.note: beheaded means the weak word loses its first letter

parts.note: sickly means weak

explanation.surface: A frail monarch is executed without delay.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something at once means doing it fast, without delay.
